sources: Fishes of Australia (Museums Victoria / OzFishNet), Bray 2022, Estuarine Stonefish, Synanceia horrida: along with the Reef Stonefish considered the most venomous of fishes; dorsal spines with venom glands at their base; venom affects the cardiovascular and neuromuscular systems; the sting is excruciatingly painful and may be fatal unless antivenom is given; an antivenom developed in 1959 reduces the likelihood of death; no deaths recorded in Australia since European arrival; superbly camouflaged ambush predator in sandy and muddy areas of sheltered coastal reefs and estuaries, often very shallow; nocturnal, feeds on small fishes, crustaceans and cephalopods; max size 60 cm; https://fishesofaustralia.net.au/home/species/3751

Sunshine Coast Council (Queensland), Stonefish on the Sunshine Coast: grow to 30 cm and are among the most venomous fish; 13 spines along their back; bumpy brown or grey skin with orange, red or green patches camouflages them among rocks or rubble, sometimes in mud or sand; live in coastal shallow waters, estuaries and creek mouths; venom causes immediate and very severe pain that may last for days, and can cause swelling, tissue damage, nausea, cardiac effects and shock; wear sturdy thick-soled shoes and shuffle your feet when wading; if stung leave the water, call for urgent medical help, remove spines and soak in water as hot as can be tolerated; antivenom may be needed; https://www.sunshinecoast.qld.gov.au/Environment/Education-Resources-and-Events/Environment-Resources-and-Publications/Coast-and-Marine/Stonefish-on-the-Sunshine-Coast

Little 1990, Emergency Medicine (Australasia) 2(4): 5, Stonefish (Synancea species) sting (James Cook University ResearchOnline): antivenom available since 1959 but rarely used; a review of antivenom use over 12 months found only 10 cases where stonefish antivenom was used; https://researchonline.jcu.edu.au/39469/

beats.say: Step on this rock, and thirteen spines full of venom go into your foot.
The pain hits right away. And it can last for days.
It's not a rock. It's a stonefish. The most venomous fish known.
Each spine has a venom gland at its base.
The venom can bring swelling, damaged skin, sickness, even shock.
Its bumpy skin hides it among rocks and rubble, in shallow water.
Would Meatball survive? With fast help, very likely. There's been an antivenom since nineteen fifty nine.
It just sits still, and waits. Then it gulps down small fish and shrimp.
It lives on reefs, in estuaries, and at creek mouths, sometimes buried in sand.
The biggest ones grow to about two feet long.
Its venom works on the heart, and the muscles.
If you're stung, get out of the water, and call for help.
Pull out any spines, and soak the foot in water as hot as you can stand.
If that's not enough, doctors give the antivenom.
It's rarely needed. One review found it used only ten times in a whole year.
In Australia, no deaths from a stonefish have been recorded.
So wear thick soled shoes, and shuffle your feet when you wade.
Would you wade barefoot on a reef?
